content: Endotracheal intubation is a frequently performed procedure in neonates, and its associated risks are well-documented. Some endotracheal tubes (ETTs) are designed with an inflatable cuff, which can be expanded after insertion into the airway to minimize air leakage or prevent aspiration. In older children and adults, cuffed ETTs have been shown to reduce gas leakage around the tube, decrease the need for tube exchanges, lower the risk of accidental extubation, and limit healthcare workers' exposure to anesthetic gases during surgical procedures. With advancements in understanding neonatal airway anatomy and the increasing use of cuffed ETTs by anesthesiologists, their application in neonates is becoming more common. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of cuffed ETTs (both inflated and non-inflated) compared to uncuffed ETTs for respiratory support in neonates. A systematic search was conducted in CENTRAL, PubMed, and CINAHL databases on August 20, 2021. Additional studies were identified through trial registries and reference lists. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and cluster-randomized trials that compared cuffed (inflated or non-inflated) versus uncuffed ETTs in neonates. The comparisons included: (1) inflated cuffed versus uncuffed ETTs, (2) non-inflated cuffed versus uncuffed ETTs, and (3) inflated cuffed versus non-inflated cuffed ETTs. The review followed Cochrane Neonatal's standard methodology. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The GRADE approach was used to determine the certainty of the evidence. Only one eligible RCT was identified for inclusion. This study compared cuffed ETTs (inflated if the ETT leak exceeded 20% with cuff pressure ≤20 cm H2O) to uncuffed ETTs. The study included 69 neonates who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. However, there was potential bias due to the lack of blinding and other methodological concerns. The evidence regarding the frequency of postextubation stridor was highly uncertain, as the confidence intervals (CIs) for the risk ratio (RR) were very wide (RR 1.36, 95% CI 0.35 to 5.25; risk difference [RD] 0.03, −0.11 to 0.18; 1 study, 69 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No neonates were diagnosed with postextubation subglottic stenosis, but endoscopic evaluation was not performed to confirm the absence of this condition. Similarly, the evidence for reintubation due to stridor or subglottic stenosis was very uncertain, with wide CIs (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.01 to 6.49; RD −0.03, 95% CI −0.11 to 0.05; 1 study, 69 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No neonates required surgical interventions, such as endoscopic balloon dilation, cricoid split, or tracheostomy, for stridor or subglottic stenosis. Neonates randomized to cuffed ETTs appeared less likely to require reintubation for any reason (RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.45; RD −0.39, 95% CI −0.57 to −0.21; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] 3, 95% CI 2 to 5; 1 study, 69 participants; very low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence for accidental extubation was also very uncertain, with wide CIs (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.12 to 5.46; RD −0.01, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.10; 1 study, 69 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence for all-cause mortality during the initial hospitalization was highly uncertain, with extremely wide CIs (RR 2.46, 95% CI 0.10 to 58.39; RD 0.03, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.10; 1 study, 69 participants; very low-certainty evidence). One ongoing trial was identified, and two additional studies were classified as awaiting classification because they did not report outcomes separately for neonates and older infants. In conclusion, the evidence comparing cuffed versus uncuffed ETTs in neonates is limited to a single RCT with a small sample size and potential bias. The certainty of the evidence for all outcomes is very low. The confidence intervals for postextubation stridor were wide, and no neonates showed clinical evidence of subglottic stenosis, although endoscopic confirmation was not available. Further RCTs are needed to assess the benefits and risks of cuffed ETTs (both inflated and non-inflated) in neonates. These studies should include neonates and evaluate both short-term use (e.g., during surgery) and long-term use (e.g., in cases of chronic lung disease).
